paragraphs: Training can impose structure on a model even when its objective contains no explicit regularization term. This paper studies that effect in multilayer homogeneous models, including fully connected and convolutional networks with linear, ReLU, or Leaky ReLU activations. Its central question is whether the optimization process itself keeps different layers balanced.

For gradient flow, the idealized version of gradient descent with infinitesimal steps, the authors prove that differences between layers’ squared weight norms stay constant. Consequently, starting with small weights automatically keeps layer magnitudes balanced. The result identifies a precise quantity preserved during training, rather than simply observing a tendency in experiments.

The authors then study finite steps in asymmetric low-rank matrix factorization. With a specified decreasing step-size schedule, gradient descent balances the two factors and converges to a bounded global optimum. For the rank-one case, a finer analysis establishes globally linear convergence with a constant step size. These matrix-factorization guarantees illustrate how the gradient-flow insight can support concrete optimization results.
neurips-2018-algorithmic-regularization-.tldr: Gradient flow preserves differences in layer weight norms, automatically balancing small initializations and motivating convergence guarantees for matrix factorization.

paragraphs: Equalized Odds evaluates fairness by comparing false-positive and false-negative rates across protected groups. Those comparisons describe disparities in predictions, but they do not explain the processes that produced them. This paper addresses the disconnect between measuring unequal error rates and determining whether those differences arise through mechanisms considered unfair.

The authors introduce a family of counterfactual measures within a nonparametric structural causal model. These measures connect differences in classification errors to underlying causal mechanisms, including mechanisms that may not be directly observed. The aim is to give analysts a way to interpret a classifier’s statistical disparities through an account of how those disparities arise.

The paper also uses these measures to develop a learning procedure described as statistically efficient, interpretable, and compatible with basic intuitions about fairness. Experiments use both synthetic data and the COMPAS dataset. The contribution connects evaluation and model construction: the same causal perspective that helps explain errors also informs how a classifier is learned.
neurips-2018-equality-of-opportunity-in-.tldr: Counterfactual measures connect unequal classification errors to causal mechanisms and support a learning procedure informed by that causal account.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can require repeated gradient calculations and communication between machines. This paper asks when previously computed gradients can remain useful enough to reuse. Its Lazily Aggregated Gradient methods, or LAG, adaptively skip some fresh calculations, reducing both computation and the communication associated with supplying new gradients.

The method uses simple rules to detect gradients that change slowly. When those rules permit it, the algorithm reuses an older gradient in the aggregate update. The theoretical analysis establishes the same convergence rate as batch gradient descent across strongly convex, convex, and nonconvex cases, showing that selective reuse can preserve the rate of optimization progress.

The communication guarantee has an additional condition: the distributed datasets must have heterogeneity captured by specified measurable constants. Under that condition, LAG reduces the communication rounds needed to reach a target accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real data also report substantial communication savings over alternatives. The result makes selective gradient refreshes a principled way to reduce distributed training costs.
neurips-2018-lag-lazily-aggregated-gradi.tldr: LAG selectively reuses older gradients to reduce distributed learning costs while preserving batch gradient descent’s convergence rate.

paragraphs: A neural network can have far more parameters than training examples and still predict well on new data. This paper investigates that behavior in small datasets, where overfitting is an especially relevant concern. It combines an empirical analysis of fitted networks with classification experiments on a broad collection of real-world datasets.

Using a linear program, the authors decompose trained networks into ensembles of subnetworks with low bias. They find that these subnetworks are relatively uncorrelated. Their proposed explanation is that this internal diversity creates a regularizing effect similar to a random forest, helping explain why a large network can resist overfitting.

The experimental study covers 116 datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, including nontrivial label noise and substantially fewer examples than typical deep-learning image tasks. Networks with hundreds of parameters per training observation achieve superior classification accuracy without overfitting in the reported study. The evidence supports the possibility of effective large-network learning on small data, alongside an empirical explanation for that behavior.
neurips-2018-modern-neural-networks-gene.tldr: Experiments suggest that relatively uncorrelated subnetworks provide internal regularization, helping large neural networks generalize on small, noisy datasets.

paragraphs: Robots trained on carefully arranged laboratory data can face a different visual world in people’s homes. This paper tackles that mismatch by collecting grasping experience directly in homes. To make collection scalable across locations, the authors build a mobile manipulator costing under 3,000 US dollars.

Affordable hardware introduces another problem: imperfect execution and calibration can make training labels noisy. The proposed learning framework represents that noise as a latent variable, allowing it to be modeled separately. Training uses 28,000 grasps gathered in several houses under varied environmental conditions, bringing both household diversity and hardware imperfections into the learning process.

Evaluation involves physically grasping new objects in homes not used for training. The authors report a 43.7% improvement over a model trained on laboratory data, while explicitly modeling latent noise yields a further reported comparison of 10% over an architecture without that mechanism. Together, these findings support collecting data in deployment-like environments and accounting for the inaccuracies of inexpensive robots.
neurips-2018-robot-learning-in-homes-imp.tldr: Home-collected grasping data and explicit modeling of hardware-induced label noise improve grasping performance in unseen homes.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient does not by itself establish that a point is near a local minimum. Saddle points can also have small gradients. This paper develops stochastic optimization algorithms that exploit third-order smoothness to escape non-degenerate saddle points more efficiently and reach an approximate local minimum.

The target has two requirements: its gradient norm is at most epsilon, and the smallest eigenvalue of its Hessian is at least minus the square root of epsilon. In plain language, the point has little first-order incentive to move and no excessively negative curvature. For unconstrained stochastic optimization, the proposed algorithm reaches this target using roughly epsilon to the power minus ten-thirds stochastic gradient evaluations, with logarithmic factors suppressed.

The stated previous bound scales as epsilon to the power minus seven-halves, so the improvement becomes more consequential as the requested tolerance shrinks. Experiments on two nonconvex problems support the method’s effectiveness and its theoretical analysis. The contribution shows how the additional third-order smoothness structure can improve the cost of finding these approximate solutions.
neurips-2018-third-order-smoothness-help.tldr: Exploiting third-order smoothness improves the stochastic gradient complexity of escaping saddle points and finding approximate local minima.

paragraphs: Optimal transport measures the cost of moving probability mass from one distribution to another, giving the Wasserstein or earth mover’s distance. This paper develops a direct algorithm for computing that quantity to a chosen additive accuracy. Its focus is both the total computation required and how much of that computation can run in parallel.

For two distributions of dimension n and accuracy epsilon, the algorithm has parallel depth of roughly 1/epsilon and total work of roughly n squared divided by epsilon, suppressing polylogarithmic factors. Parallel depth describes the sequential stages that remain even when work is distributed. The method uses primal-dual extragradient updates, motivated by theoretical advances in maximum flow.

Earlier reduction-based algorithms achieved the same work bound through positive linear programming or matrix scaling. The new approach matches that bound while either improving parallelization or avoiding linear-system solves required by those routes. It also improves the stated bounds for previous first-order methods. The contribution therefore concerns the computational structure of achieving accurate transport solutions, alongside the work guarantee.
neurips-2019-a-direct-tilde-o-1-epsilon-.tldr: A direct extragradient algorithm computes optimal transport with strong work bounds while improving parallelization or avoiding linear-system solves.

paragraphs: Multichannel sparse blind deconvolution seeks to recover a shared kernel and several sparse input signals from their observed convolutions. Both the kernel and the original inputs are unknown. This paper studies the circulant convolution setting and formulates recovery as a nonconvex optimization problem constrained to a sphere.

The proposed solver is ordinary Riemannian gradient descent, which performs gradient-based optimization while respecting that spherical constraint. Under mild statistical assumptions on the data, the authors prove that random initialization followed by this method recovers both the kernel and the signals. Recovery is qualified by a signed shift ambiguity, so the guarantee allows that remaining equivalence between recovered solutions.

Compared with prior state-of-the-art results, the paper reports improvements in sample complexity and computational efficiency. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theory and show superior performance over earlier methods. The significance is that a relatively direct optimization procedure has a recovery guarantee under the stated assumptions, despite the nonconvex formulation and the need to estimate multiple unknown components jointly.
neurips-2019-a-nonconvex-approach-for-ex.tldr: Under statistical assumptions, Riemannian gradient descent recovers a shared convolution kernel and sparse signals up to a signed shift ambiguity.

paragraphs: Descriptions of neural-network minima often distinguish sharp regions from flat ones. This paper argues that the geometry can also be asymmetric: along a direction through a minimum, loss may rise steeply on one side and gradually on the other. The authors formalize regions with many such directions as asymmetric valleys.

Under assumptions described as mild, they prove that a solution displaced toward the flatter side can generalize better than the exact minimizer of training loss. This connects the shape surrounding a minimum to where a useful solution should lie. The conclusion is conditional on the analysis, and concerns generalization rather than simply obtaining the lowest empirical loss.

The paper then shows that averaging weights along a stochastic gradient descent trajectory implicitly produces this kind of displacement. That offers a theoretical explanation for previously observed benefits associated with averaging. Experiments on modern deep networks and simple two-layer networks examine the assumptions and properties of these valleys, supporting a more directional account of loss geometry and its relationship to generalization.
neurips-2019-asymmetric-valleys-beyond-s.tldr: Under mild assumptions, moving toward the flatter side of an asymmetric loss valley improves generalization, and weight averaging induces such a bias.

paragraphs: Many learning procedures assess an observation by calculating its likelihood under a proposed distribution. When that distribution was estimated from data, errors in the estimate can affect the assessment. This paper proposes accounting for that uncertainty by considering a neighborhood of distributions around each nominal estimate.

The authors call this neighborhood an ambiguity set. They define the optimistic likelihood as the largest likelihood that the observation receives under any distribution in that set. The resulting score therefore reflects the most favorable explanation available within the allowed neighborhood. The neighborhood’s definition is central because it determines which alternative distributions can participate in the calculation.

When proximity is measured using Fisher-Rao distance or Kullback-Leibler divergence, the authors show that the resulting optimization can be handled efficiently through geodesic or ordinary convex methods. Classification experiments on synthetic and empirical data illustrate advantages of using these scores. The contribution brings uncertainty about an estimated distribution into likelihood evaluation while providing computationally tractable formulations for the stated choices of proximity.
neurips-2019-calculating-optimistic-like.tldr: Optimistic likelihoods account for distribution-estimation uncertainty by maximizing likelihood over a nearby set that admits efficient convex optimization.

paragraphs: An agent with many skills would benefit from combining what it already knows into longer tasks. Learning every possible combination independently would be impractical. This paper introduces compositional plan vectors, or CPVs, as representations that help a demonstration-conditioned policy reuse learned behavior when facing new compositions of tasks.

A CPV represents a trajectory as the sum of its constituent subtasks. The authors show that these representations can be learned through one-shot imitation learning without extra supervision or information specifying a task hierarchy. This matters because the compositional structure is learned within the imitation framework instead of requiring separately supplied descriptions of how each task breaks down.

The reported policy generalizes to tasks sequencing twice as many skills as those encountered during training. The vectors also support arithmetic: adding the representations of two tasks can command their composition without further training. These findings show that the learned representation can serve both as a description of demonstrated behavior and as a means of specifying new combinations.
neurips-2019-compositional-plan-vectors-.tldr: Compositional plan vectors let an imitation-learning policy combine tasks through vector arithmetic and generalize to longer skill sequences.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification asks a model to recognize new classes from only a handful of labeled examples. This paper identifies a weakness in approaches that extract features from labeled examples and unlabeled queries independently: those features may not emphasize what distinguishes the particular classes being compared.

The proposed Cross Attention Network makes the comparison influence the features. For each pairing of a class representation and a query representation, a cross-attention module creates maps that highlight relevant object regions. This helps focus the comparison on visual evidence useful for recognizing the target class, addressing the challenge of classes that were unseen during training.

A second component tackles the shortage of labeled data through transductive inference. It repeatedly uses the unlabeled query set to augment the support set, making class representations more representative. Experiments on two benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art methods and describe the framework as computationally efficient. The approach combines more selective comparisons with information drawn from the collection of queries being classified.
neurips-2019-cross-attention-network-for.tldr: Cross-attention sharpens class–query comparisons, while transductive updates use unlabeled queries to strengthen few-shot class representations.

paragraphs: Deep Equilibrium Models approach sequence modeling by solving directly for a stable hidden representation. The motivation is the observation that hidden layers in many deep sequence models tend toward a fixed point. A root-finding procedure locates that equilibrium, corresponding to an infinitely deep feedforward network whose layers share weights.

Training differentiates through the equilibrium using implicit differentiation. This allows training and prediction to use constant memory with respect to the network’s effective depth. That qualification matters: the memory claim concerns depth, and the method’s central advantage is obtaining the equilibrium representation without retaining a growing sequence of layer states.

The authors apply the approach to self-attention transformers and trellis networks. On large-scale language-modeling tasks, including WikiText-103, DEQs often improve performance at similar parameter counts while requiring comparable computation. The reported experiments reduce memory consumption by as much as 88%. The findings position equilibrium computation as a way to retain the modeling benefits of effective depth while substantially reducing its memory demands.
neurips-2019-deep-equilibrium-models-bc9.tldr: Deep Equilibrium Models solve for fixed-point representations and differentiate implicitly, enabling constant memory with respect to effective depth.

paragraphs: Dynamic Time Warping compares signals while accommodating changes in their timing. This can make its discrepancy measurements more meaningful when corresponding signal patterns are stretched or compressed along the time axis. DTWNet brings that property into a neural-network component intended to improve the features extracted from data.

The paper’s emphasis is on the role DTW plays inside learning. Previous successful uses had treated it as a loss function; here, the framework uses DTW for feature extraction itself. The timing-aware comparison therefore helps shape the representation produced by the network, making alignment part of the process of obtaining useful features.

The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the DTW loss and propose a stochastic backpropagation scheme intended to improve the accuracy and efficiency of DTW learning. They demonstrate an additional use of the framework as a data-analysis tool for decomposition. Together, these contributions connect a signal-comparison method, a learning procedure, and an analysis application within the same proposed framework.
neurips-2019-dtwnet-a-dynamic-time-warpi.tldr: DTWNet incorporates Dynamic Time Warping into feature extraction and proposes stochastic backpropagation for learning with that component.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible models whose capacity grows with the data, but standard exact inference becomes computationally demanding as datasets expand. This paper develops a scalable computational approach that makes exact Gaussian-process training possible on more than a million points, substantially extending the scale discussed for standard procedures.

The approach combines multiple GPUs with methods such as linear conjugate gradients. It accesses the kernel matrix through matrix multiplication and partitions those multiplications across devices. This organization distributes the expensive computation while retaining the exact Gaussian-process model. The method is broadly applicable: it does not require data arranged on a grid or restrict use to particular kernel classes.

The increased scale enables comparisons between exact Gaussian processes and scalable approximations on datasets ranging from ten thousand to one million points. The authors report dramatic performance improvements in those comparisons. The contribution is therefore both computational and empirical: it makes a previously difficult model feasible at larger scales and uses that capability to examine the performance consequences of approximation.
neurips-2019-exact-gaussian-processes-on.tldr: Distributed kernel-matrix multiplication and iterative methods enable exact Gaussian-process training on more than a million data points.

paragraphs: Memory appears in many reinforcement-learning agents, but its presence alone does not explain when a particular memory system helps. This paper focuses on evaluating that question systematically. It asks how well agents transfer what they learn to held-out tasks that differ along dimensions relevant to memory use.

The authors construct a diverse suite of memory tasks designed to test generalization across multiple dimensions. This makes the relationship between training and evaluation an explicit part of the methodology. The intended assessment concerns whether learned behavior remains useful when the held-out setting changes in ways selected to probe memory-specific generalization.

The paper also develops an agent architecture combining multiple memory systems and studies it through several ablations and baseline models. Removing or changing components provides a way to investigate their contributions within the task suite. The stated contribution is an evaluation methodology and accompanying architectural investigation, giving researchers a structured way to study working and episodic memory rather than treating memory as a single undifferentiated capability.
neurips-2019-generalization-of-reinforce.tldr: A diverse task suite and agent ablations provide a systematic methodology for evaluating how reinforcement-learning memory systems generalize.

paragraphs: Prototype methods represent prediction targets using reference vectors. This paper places those vectors on a hypersphere and uses that shared output geometry for both classification and regression. For classification, class prototypes are positioned in advance with large separation, instead of being calculated as averages of training examples.

The prototype placement comes from data-independent optimization, with an extension that incorporates prior information about class semantics. Because the prototypes are fixed, they need no updating during training. The construction accommodates any training-set size and releases the output dimensionality from a requirement to equal the number of classes, giving the representation a different relationship to the prediction task.

For regression, the network’s output is optimized as an interpolation between two prototypes on the sphere. Classification and regression consequently share a loss function and can be trained jointly in multitask problems. Experiments report benefits across classification, regression, and their combination compared with other prototype methods, softmax cross-entropy, and mean-squared-error approaches. The central contribution is a common geometric formulation for these prediction settings.
neurips-2019-hyperspherical-prototype-ne.tldr: Fixed prototypes on a hypersphere give classification and regression a shared geometry and loss function for joint training.

paragraphs: Evaluating an image generator involves two questions: whether its outputs have high quality and whether they cover the variety present in real data. This paper proposes a metric that measures those aspects separately. It builds explicit, nonparametric representations of the manifolds occupied by real and generated samples.

The authors demonstrate the metric using StyleGAN and BigGAN, including examples where existing measures give uninformative or conflicting results. Separating quality from coverage makes the evaluation more informative about the properties of a generated distribution. The paper then applies this perspective to different StyleGAN designs to examine how architecture and training choices affect their outputs.

That analysis identifies new variants reported to improve the state of the art. The authors also analyze truncation methods and identify an improved approach. Finally, they extend the metric to assess the perceptual quality of individual samples and use it to study latent-space interpolations. The contribution combines a more differentiated evaluation tool with applications to model design and the behavior of generated samples.
neurips-2019-improved-precision-and-reca.tldr: A precision-and-recall metric separately assesses generated-image quality and coverage, supporting analyses of model design, truncation, and interpolation.

paragraphs: Meta-learning transfers knowledge across tasks, often through shared parameters or optimization procedures. This paper makes relationships more explicit by using a graph connecting output classes. Its Gated Propagation Network, or GPN, aims to help classes with little training data benefit from observations associated with related classes.

The method works with class prototypes, reference representations used for nearest-neighbor classification. GPN learns to exchange messages between prototypes along graph connections. Attention combines messages from neighboring classes, while a gate chooses between that aggregate and information from the class itself. This creates a learned mechanism for incorporating related-class evidence into each prototype.

Training proceeds through sampled subgraphs and a sequence of tasks ranging from many-shot to few-shot. Stored prototypes can be reused and updated across this process, supporting a continuing learning cycle. On two benchmark datasets, GPN outperforms recent meta-learning methods under varied training–test discrepancies and test-task constructions. The results support explicitly modeling class relationships as a useful source of information for few-shot learning.
neurips-2019-learning-to-propagate-for-g.tldr: Gated Propagation Networks improve few-shot class prototypes by learning how to exchange information across a graph of related classes.

paragraphs: This paper studies the best classification accuracy possible when an adversary can modify test examples. The setting has two classes, and each modification must remain within an allowed neighborhood. The goal is to characterize a fundamental performance limit that can serve as a reference for evaluating robust classifiers.

The authors define an optimal-transport cost between the two class distributions whose minimum determines the smallest achievable adversarial zero-one loss over all classifiers. When prediction is restricted to a particular hypothesis class, the transport quantity provides a lower bound on that loss. This links adversarial classification to a problem of transporting probability mass between distributions.

For Gaussian data with norm-bounded adversaries, the paper gives matching classification and transport bounds and establishes the optimality of linear classifiers in that setting. It also characterizes learning sample complexity. Finally, the framework studies the gap between optimal possible performance and robust neural networks on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and CIFAR-10. These applications connect fundamental limits to both a structured theoretical case and empirical model assessment.
neurips-2019-lower-bounds-on-adversarial.tldr: Optimal transport characterizes the minimum adversarial classification loss and provides a benchmark for assessing achievable robustness.

paragraphs: Combining observations becomes difficult when sources measure at different spatial or temporal resolutions, have different noise levels, and may depend on one another. This paper introduces a multi-resolution, multitask Gaussian-process framework for integrating such evidence. It accommodates differences in resolution and fidelity both within an individual task and across tasks.

The authors develop two kinds of construction. Shallow Gaussian-process mixtures replace a difficult joint likelihood with a composite likelihood, making the integration problem more manageable. Deep Gaussian-process constructions handle biases naturally. The framework also includes information-theoretic corrections and efficient variational approximations, providing tools for carrying out inference in these models.

The paper demonstrates competitive performance in synthetic settings and in estimating air pollution at highly local scales across London. That application combines multiple sensing modalities operating at different spatial and temporal resolutions. The contribution is a modeling framework suited to this uneven evidence: it represents differences in how observations are collected while allowing their information to contribute to related estimation tasks.
neurips-2019-multi-resolution-multi-task.tldr: A Gaussian-process framework integrates potentially dependent observations collected at different resolutions, fidelities, and noise levels.

paragraphs: This paper studies distributed estimation with an especially tight communication budget. Each of m machines observes n independent, identically distributed samples and sends one message to a server. The message length grows only logarithmically with mn, and the server must estimate a parameter minimizing expected loss from these messages.

The proposed Multi-Resolution Estimator has expected error bounded, up to polylogarithmic factors, by m to the power minus one over max(d, 2), multiplied by n to the power minus one-half. Here d is the parameter dimension. This dependence shows how the machine count, local sample count, and dimensionality enter the guarantee. The bound matches existing lower bounds up to those logarithmic factors.

A distinctive consequence is that expected error approaches zero as the number of machines increases even when each machine’s sample count stays bounded by a constant. The paper contrasts this property with existing algorithms. It makes the method relevant to settings with many machines holding very little data, while retaining the one-message-per-machine restriction.
neurips-2019-order-optimal-one-shot-dist.tldr: A one-shot distributed estimator achieves near-optimal error rates and remains consistent as machines increase despite bounded local sample counts.

paragraphs: Asynchronous optimization lets parallel workers make progress without exact synchronization, but proving useful guarantees becomes harder with richer objectives and constraints. This paper introduces ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG for sparse online and stochastic optimization. Their analyses extend beyond coordinate-wise box constraints and objectives that are both smooth and strongly convex.

ASYNCADA handles generic convex constraints, proximal updates for composite objectives, and adaptive step sizes. It has finite-time, data-dependent guarantees and anytime convergence guarantees without requiring an exact global clock. With sufficiently sparse data, its convergence rate matches the corresponding serial rate across several objective classes, including a limited nonconvex class, yielding a theoretical linear speedup.

HEDGEHOG is an asynchronous parallel form of Exponentiated Gradient for optimization over the probability simplex. It likewise achieves linear speedups under sparsity, extending this benefit to updates outside the usual stochastic-gradient form. A common analysis framework underlies both algorithms and also applies to distributed optimization and delayed feedback. Sparsity is therefore a stated condition enabling the speedup results across these broader settings.
neurips-2019-think-out-of-the-box-generi.tldr: ASYNCADA and HEDGEHOG extend asynchronous optimization guarantees to broader constraints and updates, with theoretical linear speedups under sparsity.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search involves choosing which operations should form a network. XNAS develops an optimization method for differentiable search using the theory of prediction with expert advice. Its criterion minimizes regret from suboptimal operation choices, giving the search process an objective directly concerned with the quality of those selections.

The method dynamically removes inferior architecture options and strengthens better ones. The authors establish an optimal worst-case regret bound and motivate using multiple learning rates according to the information carried by backward gradients. These are guarantees and design choices for the architecture-selection process; the empirical classification results provide a separate assessment of the architectures obtained.

Experiments report strong image-classification performance across several datasets. The stated error rates are 1.6% on CIFAR-10 and 23.9% on ImageNet under mobile settings, alongside state-of-the-art results on three additional datasets. The paper therefore connects a theoretically motivated selection rule to practical architecture search, with reported evidence that this way of allocating emphasis among candidate operations can produce competitive networks.
neurips-2019-xnas-neural-architecture-se.tldr: XNAS uses expert-advice theory to guide differentiable architecture selection, combining an optimal regret bound with strong reported classification results.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel. This paper introduces a zero-shot version of the task, in which a model must label object categories that have no training examples. The setting includes both previously seen and unseen categories at test time, so the model must handle them together.

The proposed ZS3Net combines a deep segmentation model with a mechanism that generates visual representations from semantic word embeddings. This links semantic descriptions of categories to the visual representations used for pixel classification. A self-training stage further improves performance by automatically assigning pseudo-labels to pixels from unseen classes and using those assignments in learning.

The authors establish zero-shot benchmarks and competitive baselines on Pascal-VOC and Pascal-Context. For complex scenes in Pascal-Context, they extend the method with graph-context encoding that uses spatial context priors from class-wise segmentation maps. The contribution combines a new evaluation task with an architecture that brings semantic information, automatically labeled pixels, and spatial context into learning to segment unseen categories.
neurips-2019-zero-shot-semantic-segmenta.tldr: ZS3Net uses semantic word embeddings to support pixel classification for unseen categories, with further improvements from self-training and spatial context.
